setup-local-envoy.q: What single tool do you actually install to run Envoy for this course?
options: Docker — Envoy itself comes as a container image you don't install directly
The Envoy binary, compiled from source
Kubernetes
A web browser only
setup-local-envoy.why: You install Docker; it pulls the envoyproxy/envoy image and the practice backend automatically. Nothing else touches your system.
whyWrong: Compiling Envoy is a heavyweight Bazel build the course never asks for — Docker pulls a prebuilt image instead.
Kubernetes doesn't appear until Module 08, and even then the labs don't have you install it.
A browser can't run containers; you need Docker to actually execute Envoy.

setup-local-envoy.q: What does 'docker compose up' do inside a lab folder?
options: Downloads and starts Envoy plus the backend defined in that folder's files
Deletes all containers on your machine
Installs Docker itself
Publishes your config to the internet
setup-local-envoy.why: Each lab folder has a docker-compose.yaml describing Envoy and a backend. 'up' pulls the images (first time) and runs them together.
whyWrong: Nothing is deleted — 'down' removes only that lab's containers, and 'up' just starts them.
Docker must already be installed; compose is a feature of Docker, not its installer.
Everything runs locally on your machine; nothing is uploaded anywhere.

setup-local-envoy.q: After Envoy is running, how do you send a test request through it?
options: Run 'curl localhost:10000' from a second terminal
Restart your computer
Edit the envoy.yaml file
Open port 9901 to the public internet
setup-local-envoy.why: The listener is bound to port 10000. Keep Envoy running in one terminal and curl it from another; you'll see a matching log line appear.
whyWrong: Restarting changes nothing — Envoy is already running and just waiting for a request.
Editing config doesn't generate traffic; you need an actual client request like curl.
9901 is the admin interface, not the traffic port — and it should never be exposed publicly.

setup-local-envoy.q: How do you stop a lab and clean up when you're done?
options: Press Ctrl-C in the Envoy terminal, then run 'docker compose down'
Just close the terminal window and hope for the best
Delete Docker
Run 'curl /quitquitquit' on every port
setup-local-envoy.why: Ctrl-C stops the running containers; 'docker compose down' removes them. Every lab starts with 'up' and ends with 'down'.
whyWrong: Closing the window can leave containers running in the background, still holding your ports.
Uninstalling Docker is wildly overkill and would break every other lab.
/quitquitquit only stops an Envoy process via its admin port; it doesn't remove the lab's containers.

primer-what-is-a-proxy.q: In one sentence, what is a proxy?
options: A middleman program that sits between a client and a server, passing requests and responses on their behalf
A server that stores a website's database
A programming language for building websites
A physical device that boosts your wifi signal
primer-what-is-a-proxy.why: Like a waiter between you and the kitchen, a proxy is a go-between: you talk to it, and it talks to the real server for you, relaying the answer back.
whyWrong: Storage is a database's job; a proxy holds conversations in transit, not data at rest.
A proxy is a running program in the network path, not a language you write code in.
It's software in the request path, not hardware for your radio signal.

primer-what-is-a-proxy.q: When you put a proxy in the middle, one direct connection becomes how many conversations?
options: Two — you-to-proxy and proxy-to-server, stitched together to feel like one
One — the proxy just watches the existing connection
Zero — the proxy removes the need to connect
Four — one for each direction on each side
primer-what-is-a-proxy.why: The proxy holds two separate conversations: it receives your request, then makes its own request to the real server, then relays the reply back to you.
whyWrong: The proxy isn't a passive observer — it terminates your connection and opens its own to the server.
Connections still happen; the proxy adds a hop, it doesn't remove the network.
Each side is one two-way conversation; requests and responses share the same connection.

primer-what-is-a-proxy.q: Which of these is a useful job a proxy can do from its spot in the middle?
options: Routing, load balancing, retries, TLS, caching, metrics, or shielding the servers
Writing the application's business logic for it
Physically cooling the server hardware
Designing the website's visual layout
primer-what-is-a-proxy.why: The middle is a great place to do work every request needs — so you build it once in the proxy instead of into every server or client.
whyWrong: Business logic stays in the application; the proxy handles cross-cutting network concerns.
A proxy is software; it has no influence on server temperature.
Page design is frontend work; a proxy only relays and shapes traffic.

primer-what-is-a-proxy.q: What is the difference between a forward proxy and a reverse proxy?
options: A forward proxy is a middleman for the client reaching out; a reverse proxy is a middleman for the servers receiving traffic
A forward proxy is faster; a reverse proxy is slower
A forward proxy uses HTTP; a reverse proxy uses HTTPS
They are the same thing
primer-what-is-a-proxy.why: Forward = sits in front of clients reaching the internet (filtering, hiding who's browsing). Reverse = sits in front of servers, taking outside traffic to the right backend.
whyWrong: Speed doesn't define them — the difference is whose side of the conversation each one represents.
Either kind can speak HTTP or HTTPS; the protocol isn't what distinguishes them.
They sit on opposite sides: one fronts clients going out, the other fronts servers taking traffic in.

primer-what-is-a-proxy.q: Which kind of proxy is Envoy, and why does it fit this course?
options: A reverse proxy — it fronts your backend services to route, balance, secure, and observe incoming traffic
A forward proxy — it filters employees' web browsing
Neither — Envoy is a database
Both, but only when running on Windows
primer-what-is-a-proxy.why: Envoy is a powerful, programmable reverse proxy. Routing incoming traffic to a fleet of services, load balancing, terminating HTTPS, retrying failures — that's the reverse-proxy job.
whyWrong: Filtering outbound browsing is the classic forward-proxy job — the opposite of what this course covers.
Envoy stores no application data; it moves requests between clients and your services.
Envoy's role has nothing to do with the OS — and its job is reverse proxying regardless.

primer-service-mesh.q: What core problem does a service mesh exist to solve?
options: It moves repetitive networking concerns — security, retries, metrics, routing — out of every app and into shared infrastructure
It makes individual services run faster on the CPU
It replaces the need for any backend services
It stores all of a company's data in one place
primer-service-mesh.why: In a big microservice system, every team keeps re-implementing the same networking logic. A mesh factors it out into infrastructure so it's done once, uniformly.
whyWrong: A mesh adds a proxy hop, so if anything it costs a little latency; the win is uniformity, not speed.
Your services still do all the real work — the mesh only handles the traffic between them.
Data storage is a database concern; a mesh carries requests, it doesn't keep them.

options: A small proxy running next to each service instance that handles all traffic in and out of that service
A backup copy of a service's database
A second CPU dedicated to networking
A special cable between two servers
primer-service-mesh.why: The service talks to its local sidecar proxy, and the proxy handles the real network. Because a proxy sits on both ends of every call, the mesh can add features uniformly.
whyWrong: It's a proxy process, not a data replica — it forwards traffic rather than storing anything.
It's software sharing the pod's existing CPU, not extra hardware.
No physical wiring involved; the sidecar intercepts traffic in software on the same host.

primer-service-mesh.q: In a mesh, what is the difference between the data plane and the control plane?
options: Data plane = the proxies carrying traffic and enforcing rules; control plane = the brain that computes config and pushes it to them
Data plane = the brain; control plane = the proxies
They are the same thing under two names
Data plane is the app; control plane is the database
primer-service-mesh.why: You state intent to the control plane once; it programs the whole fleet of proxies (the data plane) to match, updating them live as services change.
whyWrong: You've got it backwards: the proxies carry the data, and the control plane does the thinking.
The split is the whole point — one part moves packets, a separate part programs it.
Both planes are mesh infrastructure; your app and database sit outside the mesh's own layers.

primer-service-mesh.q: What is Envoy's role in a typical service mesh?
options: It's the data-plane proxy that most meshes use; the meshes differ mainly in their control plane
It is the control-plane brain that replaces Istio
It is the database every service shares
It has no role in a mesh
primer-service-mesh.why: Istio, Consul, Gloo, App Mesh and others drive Envoy as the thing on the wire, via the standard xDS API. Learn Envoy and you understand the engine inside nearly all of them.
whyWrong: Envoy is what Istio programs, not a competitor to it — istiod is the brain, Envoy is the muscle.
Envoy carries requests between services; it stores nothing.
Envoy is the most common mesh data plane — the engine inside Istio, Consul Connect, and others.

primer-service-mesh.q: Does every system need a full service mesh?
options: No — an edge gateway plus basic retries often suffices; a mesh pays off once you have many services
Yes — no system can run without a mesh
Only systems written in Go can use one
A mesh is required by Kubernetes
primer-service-mesh.why: A mesh earns its complexity at scale. For a handful of services, a single Envoy at the edge is often plenty. Newer 'ambient' modes exist to lower a mesh's cost.
whyWrong: Plenty of systems run fine with just an edge proxy; a mesh is a scale tool, not a prerequisite.
Meshes are language-agnostic — that's the selling point; the proxy doesn't care what wrote the request.
Kubernetes runs happily without any mesh; a mesh is an optional layer on top.

00-what-is-envoy.q: What is a proxy, in one sentence?
options: A program that sits between a client and a server, relaying requests and responses on the client's behalf
A database that stores every request a server receives
A programming language for writing network servers
A physical cable that connects two computers directly
00-what-is-envoy.why: A proxy sits in the middle: the client talks to the proxy, and the proxy talks to the real server for it, then relays the answer back. That middle spot is where Envoy does routing, TLS, retries, and more.
whyWrong: A proxy relays traffic in flight; persisting requests is a log or database's job.
It's a running network program, not a language for writing servers.
It's software in the path, not hardware connecting machines.

00-what-is-envoy.q: What can an L7 (application-layer) proxy do that an L4 (transport-layer) proxy cannot?
options: Read and act on the actual HTTP request — its path, headers, and method
Forward raw TCP connections faster
Use less memory per connection
Run without any configuration at all
00-what-is-envoy.why: L4 only sees bytes flowing between IP:port pairs. L7 parses the protocol (HTTP/gRPC), so it can make decisions based on the URL path, headers, and method — Envoy's superpower.
whyWrong: Raw TCP forwarding speed is the L4 proxy's advantage, not something L7 adds.
Parsing HTTP costs more memory, not less — the tradeoff buys smarts.
Both kinds need configuration; L7 typically needs more of it, not none.

00-what-is-envoy.q: Which describes the data plane vs the control plane, and which one is Envoy?
options: The data plane moves the traffic; the control plane decides the config. Envoy is the data plane.
The data plane decides config; the control plane moves traffic. Envoy is the control plane.
They are two names for the same thing; Envoy is both.
The control plane is the client and the data plane is the server.
00-what-is-envoy.why: Envoy is the thing that actually touches your traffic (data plane). A separate 'brain' (control plane, like Istio) computes config and pushes it to Envoy. Envoy consumes config; it doesn't compute it.
whyWrong: Reversed: config flows from the control plane down to Envoy, which moves the actual traffic.
They're deliberately separate roles — Envoy consumes config, it never computes it.
The planes describe infrastructure roles, not who initiates a request.

00-what-is-envoy.q: Which three roles can the same Envoy binary play?
options: Edge/API gateway, sidecar, and middle proxy
Compiler, linker, and debugger
Client, server, and database
Firewall, router, and switch
00-what-is-envoy.why: It's the same tool in all three — only the topology and who configures it differ: at the front door (edge), next to every service (sidecar/mesh), or between internal tiers (middle proxy).
whyWrong: Those are build-toolchain roles; Envoy is a proxy, not a development tool.
Envoy is always the middleman — it's neither the app tiers nor the data store.
Those are network hardware boxes; Envoy's three roles are all proxy topologies.

00-what-is-envoy.q: What is Envoy's headline advantage over classic proxies like nginx for microservices?
options: Live, dynamic reconfiguration with no restarts and zero dropped connections, via its xDS API
It is written in a faster programming language
It requires no configuration files
It can only be used inside Kubernetes
00-what-is-envoy.why: A control plane can reprogram thousands of Envoys continuously — add a route, change a backend, rotate a cert — without restarting. That's the reason service meshes chose Envoy.
whyWrong: C++ vs C isn't the story — nginx is plenty fast; the difference is how config gets updated.
Envoy needs config like any proxy; the point is that config can arrive live over xDS.
Envoy predates its Kubernetes fame and runs anywhere — VMs, bare metal, Docker.

01-architecture-and-request-lifecycle.q: Put these in the order a request flows through them: cluster, listener, route, filter chain, endpoint.
options: listener → filter chain → route → cluster → endpoint
cluster → endpoint → route → listener → filter chain
route → listener → cluster → filter chain → endpoint
endpoint → cluster → filter chain → route → listener
01-architecture-and-request-lifecycle.why: A connection arrives at a listener, flows through a filter chain, the router reads the route table to pick a cluster, and the cluster load-balances to one endpoint. That sentence is Envoy.
whyWrong: That runs backwards — clusters and endpoints are chosen last, after routing, not first.
Routing happens inside the listener's filter chain, not before the connection is accepted.
The endpoint is the final destination; nothing starts there.

01-architecture-and-request-lifecycle.q: What does the HTTP Connection Manager (HCM) do, and where does it sit?
options: It is a network filter that parses the raw byte stream into HTTP requests and hosts the HTTP filter chain
It is a separate program that runs before Envoy starts
It is the cluster that holds all the backend endpoints
It is the admin interface on port 9901
01-architecture-and-request-lifecycle.why: The HCM lives inside a listener's filter chain. It turns raw bytes into structured HTTP and runs the ordered HTTP filters (ending in the router). Everything HTTP happens inside the HCM.
whyWrong: The HCM is a filter inside Envoy's listener, not an external process.
Clusters describe backends; the HCM parses incoming HTTP on the listener side.
The admin interface is a separate server on 9901; the HCM processes real traffic.

01-architecture-and-request-lifecycle.q: Is a browser connecting to Envoy considered upstream or downstream?
options: Downstream — it is on the client side, the one that connected TO Envoy
Upstream — it is on the backend side
Neither — browsers are not part of Envoy's model
Both at the same time
01-architecture-and-request-lifecycle.why: Downstream = the client side (who connected to Envoy). Upstream = the backend side (who Envoy connects to). So 'downstream_rq_total' counts requests received from clients.
whyWrong: Upstream is the backend side — where Envoy sends requests, not where they come from.
Anything that connects to Envoy is in the model, and a browser is a downstream client.
A single peer sits on one side: the browser connects TO Envoy, making it downstream only.

01-architecture-and-request-lifecycle.q: Envoy has two independent filter pipelines. What are they?
options: The L4 network filter chain, and the L7 HTTP filter chain inside the HCM
The inbound firewall and the outbound firewall
The static pipeline and the dynamic pipeline
The request logger and the response logger
01-architecture-and-request-lifecycle.why: The network (L4) filter chain operates on the connection; inside the HCM, the HTTP (L7) filter chain operates on each request. Most of your day-to-day config lives in the HTTP filters and route table.
whyWrong: Envoy has no firewall pair; the split is by protocol layer — connection vs request.
Static vs dynamic is about config delivery, not the filter pipelines.
Logging is one feature, not a pipeline; the two chains are L4 network and L7 HTTP filters.

01-architecture-and-request-lifecycle.q: Between static and dynamic (xDS) config, what actually changes — the objects or the delivery?
options: Only the delivery — a cluster is a cluster whether it came from a file or a control-plane push
Only the objects — dynamic config uses completely different resource types
Both the objects and the delivery are entirely different
Nothing changes; static and dynamic are just two names for the same file
01-architecture-and-request-lifecycle.why: The objects (listeners, routes, clusters, endpoints) are identical either way. Master the static objects first and dynamic config is just 'the same objects, delivered over the network.'
whyWrong: The resource types are identical either way — an xDS cluster is the same object as a file cluster.
Only delivery changes; the listener/route/cluster/endpoint objects stay the same.
They're genuinely different delivery mechanisms — file at boot vs streamed at runtime.

02-lab-first-static-config.q: In the config, which section says 'accept traffic on port 10000'?
options: The listener's address block
The cluster's load_assignment
The admin interface
The router HTTP filter
02-lab-first-static-config.why: A listener binds an address+port (here 0.0.0.0:10000). That's where clients connect. Clusters describe backends, not the port Envoy listens on.
whyWrong: load_assignment lists backend addresses Envoy connects OUT to, not the port it accepts on.
The admin block binds 9901 for debugging, not the traffic port.
The router picks a cluster for a request; it has nothing to do with binding ports.

02-lab-first-static-config.q: Where does the decision 'send / to the echo_service cluster' live?
options: In the route config inside the HTTP Connection Manager
In the cluster definition
In the admin block
In the Docker Compose file
02-lab-first-static-config.why: Routes live in the route_config inside the HCM: a match (e.g. prefix: /) paired with an action (route to a cluster). The cluster just describes where the backend is.
whyWrong: The cluster says where echo_service lives, not which requests should go to it.
The admin block only configures the debug interface.
Compose starts the containers; it knows nothing about Envoy's routing rules.

02-lab-first-static-config.q: Why must the router be the last HTTP filter?
options: It forwards the request upstream, so every other filter must get to act before it
It is the slowest filter and should run when nothing else is waiting
Envoy sorts filters alphabetically and 'router' comes last
It has to run first, not last — the premise is wrong
02-lab-first-static-config.why: The router applies the route decision and sends the request to a backend. Any filter that wants to inspect or modify the request (auth, CORS, etc.) must run before that hand-off.
whyWrong: Filter order is about semantics, not speed scheduling.
Order is exactly what you write in http_filters — Envoy never sorts it.
If it ran first, no other filter could touch the request before it left for the backend.

02-lab-first-static-config.q: What did 'type: STRICT_DNS' do for the echo_service cluster?
options: Resolved the backend hostname via DNS and used every IP it returned as an endpoint
Encrypted the connection to the backend with TLS
Restricted the cluster to a single hard-coded IP address
Turned off health checking
02-lab-first-static-config.why: STRICT_DNS means 'resolve this hostname and use all returned IPs, re-resolving periodically.' Docker's internal DNS resolved 'backend' to the echo container.
whyWrong: TLS to backends is configured on the cluster's transport_socket, not its discovery type.
That's the opposite — STRICT_DNS follows DNS answers and can yield several endpoints.
Health checking is a separate cluster setting; the discovery type doesn't touch it.

02-lab-first-static-config.q: If two routes both match a request, which one wins?
options: The first one listed — route order matters
The most specific one, regardless of order
The last one listed
Envoy returns an error when two routes match
02-lab-first-static-config.why: Envoy takes the first matching route. That's why specific routes (like /healthz) must go ABOVE the catch-all prefix: / — the single most common routing bug.
whyWrong: Envoy does no specificity ranking — it's strictly top-to-bottom order.
The last one never gets a look once an earlier route matches.
Overlapping routes are normal and legal; the first match simply wins.

03-listeners-filter-chains-tls.q: What single filter turns a listener into an HTTP listener?
options: The HTTP Connection Manager — swap it for tcp_proxy and the listener becomes an L4 forwarder
The router filter
The transport_socket
The admin filter
03-listeners-filter-chains-tls.why: A listener is protocol-agnostic. Its filter chain's network filter decides behavior: http_connection_manager makes it L7/HTTP; tcp_proxy makes it a dumb-but-fast L4 forwarder.
whyWrong: The router is an HTTP filter that lives INSIDE the HCM — it needs the HCM to exist first.
The transport_socket handles TLS on the connection; it doesn't parse HTTP.
There is no admin filter; the admin interface is a separate server entirely.

03-listeners-filter-chains-tls.q: How does one :443 listener serve two different sites with different certificates?
options: Multiple filter chains, selected per connection by filter_chain_match on the SNI hostname
One filter chain that guesses the site from the request body
It cannot — you need a separate listener per site
By running two copies of Envoy on the same port
03-listeners-filter-chains-tls.why: SNI (Server Name Indication) is the hostname the client requests inside the TLS handshake. filter_chain_match on server_names picks the matching chain (and its cert/backend).
whyWrong: The cert must be chosen during the TLS handshake — before any request body exists to read.
One listener handles it fine; that's exactly what filter_chain_match is for.
Two processes can't bind the same port; SNI matching within one listener is the mechanism.

03-listeners-filter-chains-tls.q: What is the difference between DownstreamTlsContext and UpstreamTlsContext?
options: Downstream = TLS toward clients (Envoy is the server, presents a cert); Upstream = TLS toward backends (Envoy is the client, verifies a cert)
Downstream is for HTTP/1.1 and Upstream is for HTTP/2
Downstream encrypts, Upstream decrypts, on the same connection
They are identical; the names are interchangeable
03-listeners-filter-chains-tls.why: Downstream faces the client (Envoy acts as TLS server). Upstream faces the backend (Envoy acts as TLS client). mTLS in a mesh uses both directions at once.
whyWrong: HTTP version negotiation is separate config; both contexts work with either version.
Every TLS connection encrypts and decrypts on both ends; the contexts differ by which side Envoy plays.
They're distinct types with distinct roles — presenting a cert as server vs verifying one as client.

options: Envoy decrypts the client's HTTPS and forwards plain HTTP to the backend
Envoy refuses all TLS connections
The backend decrypts TLS and Envoy only forwards bytes
TLS is disabled entirely
03-listeners-filter-chains-tls.why: Envoy holds the cert, does the crypto, and speaks plain HTTP inward. That's the classic edge-gateway job: one place holds the certificates and the backends stay simple.
whyWrong: Termination means accepting and completing TLS, not rejecting it.
Backend-side decryption is TLS passthrough — the opposite arrangement.
TLS is fully active on the client side; it just ends at Envoy instead of the backend.

03-listeners-filter-chains-tls.q: Which part of the config handles encryption, and which handles HTTP routing?
options: The transport_socket handles encryption; the HCM filters handle HTTP routing — transport vs application, kept separate
The route_config handles both
The cluster handles encryption; the listener handles routing
The admin interface handles both
03-listeners-filter-chains-tls.why: TLS is a transport-layer concern (transport_socket) layered UNDER the HTTP processing (the HCM's filters and routes). That separation is a recurring Envoy theme.
whyWrong: route_config only maps requests to clusters; it never touches crypto.
Backwards — encryption lives in the listener's transport_socket, routing in the HCM.
The admin interface observes Envoy; it doesn't process or encrypt traffic.

04-http-routing-and-filters.q: Two routes match a request. Which is used?
options: The first one listed
The most specific one
The last one listed
A random one
04-http-routing-and-filters.why: First match wins. Put specific routes above general ones; a catch-all prefix: / at the top will silently shadow everything below it.
whyWrong: Envoy never ranks by specificity — order in the list is the only tiebreaker.
Later routes are shadowed the moment an earlier one matches.
Route selection is fully deterministic: top to bottom, first hit.

04-http-routing-and-filters.q: Besides a path prefix, what else can a route's match test?
options: Exact path, a regex, headers, and query parameters
Only the client's IP address
Only the time of day
Only the response status code
04-http-routing-and-filters.why: match can test exact path, safe_regex, headers (exact/prefix/regex/presence), and query_parameters — enabling canaries, API versioning, and auth gating.
whyWrong: Client IP alone isn't a route matcher — and matching is far richer than any one field.
There's no time-of-day matcher in route config.
Routing happens before the backend answers — the response status doesn't exist yet.

04-http-routing-and-filters.q: What is the difference between direct_response and redirect?
options: direct_response makes Envoy answer with a body itself; redirect tells the client to go elsewhere with a 3xx
They are the same thing
direct_response is for HTTPS only; redirect is for HTTP only
redirect answers with a body; direct_response sends a 3xx
04-http-routing-and-filters.why: direct_response = Envoy serves a canned body with no backend (health checks, maintenance pages). redirect = a 301/302 sending the client somewhere else.
whyWrong: One serves content itself; the other bounces the client — different actions entirely.
Both work regardless of protocol; HTTPS vs HTTP has nothing to do with it.
You've swapped them: redirect sends the 3xx, direct_response serves the body.

04-http-routing-and-filters.q: Why must the router filter be last in the http_filters list?
options: It forwards the request upstream, so all filters before it must run first
It logs the response, which must happen last
Envoy requires filters in alphabetical order
It must actually be first, not last
04-http-routing-and-filters.why: The router is the hand-off to the backend. Filters like cors, jwt_authn, and fault must run before that hand-off to inspect, modify, or reject the request.
whyWrong: Access logging is the HCM's job, not the router's — and it isn't why the router goes last.
You choose the order explicitly; Envoy never alphabetizes filters.
First would ship the request upstream before auth, CORS, or fault filters ever ran.

04-http-routing-and-filters.q: What is the fault filter for?
options: Injecting latency or aborts to test resilience (chaos testing) without touching real backends
Fixing broken YAML in the config
Automatically retrying failed requests
Compressing responses
04-http-routing-and-filters.why: The fault filter deliberately delays or aborts a percentage of matching requests, so teams can verify that CALLERS handle failures (retries, fallbacks) — chaos engineering as config.
whyWrong: Nothing repairs config at runtime — bad YAML simply fails to load.
Retries live in the route's retry_policy; fault does the opposite, injecting failures.
Compression is the compressor filter's job; fault only delays or aborts requests.

options: An upstream service: its endpoints plus how to balance across and health-check them
A single physical server
A port that Envoy listens on
A TLS certificate
05-clusters-load-balancing-resilience.why: If routes answer 'where does this request go?', clusters answer 'which instance, and what if it's down?' — a named group of endpoints plus load-balancing and health policy.
whyWrong: One server is just an endpoint; a cluster is the named group plus its policies.
Listening ports belong to listeners — clusters describe where traffic goes out, not in.
Certs live in transport_sockets and SDS; a cluster may reference one but isn't one.

05-clusters-load-balancing-resilience.q: When would you use STRICT_DNS vs EDS for endpoint discovery?
options: STRICT_DNS resolves a DNS name locally; EDS receives endpoints pushed by a control plane over xDS — EDS for dynamic mesh environments
STRICT_DNS is for HTTPS; EDS is for HTTP
They are identical
STRICT_DNS is dynamic; EDS is static
05-clusters-load-balancing-resilience.why: STRICT_DNS is great for Docker/K8s service names Envoy can resolve itself. EDS is how a control plane keeps up with pods appearing and disappearing in a mesh.
whyWrong: Discovery type and TLS are orthogonal — either can carry either protocol.
They differ fundamentally: local DNS resolution vs control-plane push.
Backwards: EDS is the dynamic, push-based one; STRICT_DNS just re-polls DNS.

05-clusters-load-balancing-resilience.q: What is the difference between active and passive health checking?
options: Active = Envoy proactively probes a path on an interval; passive (outlier detection) = ejects an endpoint after real 5xx/connection errors
Active checks HTTP; passive checks TCP
Active runs once at startup; passive never runs
They are two names for the same feature
05-clusters-load-balancing-resilience.why: Active health checks catch a sick backend before a user hits it. Outlier detection reacts to real traffic failures. Together they keep bad endpoints out of rotation.
whyWrong: Both styles can watch HTTP or TCP; the real split is probing vs reacting to live traffic.
Active checks repeat on an interval forever, and passive ejection runs continuously.
They're separate, complementary mechanisms — probe ahead vs react to real failures.

05-clusters-load-balancing-resilience.q: Which load-balancing policy gives you session affinity (sticky routing)?
options: RING_HASH or MAGLEV — consistent hashing on a key like a header or cookie
ROUND_ROBIN
RANDOM
LEAST_REQUEST
05-clusters-load-balancing-resilience.why: Consistent-hashing policies (RING_HASH/MAGLEV) send requests with the same key to the same backend. Round-robin, random, and least-request spread traffic without affinity.
whyWrong: Round-robin deliberately rotates through endpoints — the opposite of stickiness.
Random picks a fresh endpoint every time; the same user lands anywhere.
Least-request follows load, so the same key goes wherever is idle, not to one home.

05-clusters-load-balancing-resilience.q: How do a timeout + retry_policy + multiple endpoints hide a single failing backend?
options: Envoy caps how long it waits, then retries the request on a different healthy endpoint
Envoy caches the last good response and returns it
Envoy shuts down until the backend recovers
Envoy returns a 503 immediately every time
05-clusters-load-balancing-resilience.why: A timeout bounds the wait; a retry_policy re-sends the failed idempotent request to another endpoint. With several endpoints, one bad instance becomes invisible to the caller.
whyWrong: Envoy doesn't serve stale responses on failure; caching is a separate concern entirely.
Envoy stays up and routes around the failure — that's the whole point of resilience config.
A 503 is what the retry policy prevents; it only surfaces if every attempt fails.

06-observability-and-admin.q: Which admin endpoint shows the full effective configuration Envoy is running?
options: /config_dump
/ready
/quitquitquit
/healthz
06-observability-and-admin.why: /config_dump returns the entire effective config as JSON — invaluable for confirming what Envoy actually loaded, especially when debugging xDS.
whyWrong: /ready just says whether Envoy can serve traffic — a one-word liveness answer.
/quitquitquit shuts Envoy down; definitely not a read-only inspection endpoint.
/healthz is a path you'd route for app health checks, not an admin config viewer.

06-observability-and-admin.q: Why must the admin port (9901) never be bound to a public address in production?
options: It exposes config and secrets-adjacent data and offers control endpoints like /quitquitquit
It is slower than the main listener
It only works over HTTPS
It would use too much bandwidth
06-observability-and-admin.why: The admin interface is powerful and unauthenticated. Anyone who reaches it can read your config and even shut Envoy down. Bind it to 127.0.0.1 in production.
whyWrong: Performance isn't the issue — the danger is unauthenticated read and control access.
It serves plain HTTP by default; the concern is exposure, not protocol.
Traffic on 9901 is tiny; the risk is what an attacker can do with it, not bandwidth.

06-observability-and-admin.q: In RED-method terms, which stats map to Rate, Errors, and Duration?
options: downstream_rq_total, downstream_rq_5xx, and the downstream_rq_time histogram
upstream_cx_active, server.memory, and server.uptime
listener_added, listener_modified, and lds.update_rejected
cluster.name, endpoint.address, and lb_policy
06-observability-and-admin.why: Rate = total requests, Errors = 5xx count, Duration = the request-time histogram. In production you scrape /stats/prometheus and graph exactly these.
whyWrong: Those are resource and liveness gauges, not the request rate/error/latency trio.
Those track listener config updates from LDS, not request traffic.
Those are config fields describing a cluster, not runtime counters at all.

06-observability-and-admin.q: What does the %RESPONSE_FLAGS% field in an access log give you?
options: A short code explaining WHY a request ended a certain way (UH, UT, NR, and so on)
The client's browser and operating system
The exact SQL query the backend ran
The amount of memory Envoy used
06-observability-and-admin.why: Response flags are the debugging goldmine: UH = no healthy upstream, UT = upstream timeout, NR = no route configured, etc. Read the flag first when something's wrong.
whyWrong: User-agent details are a different log field; flags describe Envoy's view of the outcome.
Envoy never sees inside the backend — it can't know what queries ran.
Memory usage lives in /stats and /memory, not in per-request access logs.

06-observability-and-admin.q: How much application code do you change to get distributed tracing across an Envoy mesh?
options: None — it's Envoy config on each hop, since every request already passes through a proxy
You must add tracing libraries to every service
You must rewrite each service in a supported language
Tracing is impossible with Envoy
06-observability-and-admin.why: Because the proxy sits on every hop, enabling a tracing block and a sampling rate gives end-to-end traces with no app code changes — a major reason teams adopt Envoy.
whyWrong: Instrumentation libraries are the pre-mesh approach — the proxy on every hop replaces them.
Tracing is language-agnostic because the proxy, not the app, emits the spans.
Far from impossible — turnkey tracing is one of Envoy's flagship features.

07-dynamic-config-xds.q: What does xDS let Envoy do that static config cannot?
options: Fetch and refresh its configuration at runtime with no restart
Run without any config at all
Serve HTTPS instead of HTTP
Use less CPU
07-dynamic-config-xds.why: xDS (the 'x Discovery Service' APIs) let Envoy subscribe to config from an external source and update live — the foundation of managing fleets of proxies.
whyWrong: Envoy always needs config; xDS changes where it comes from, not whether it exists.
TLS works fine with static config; xDS is about delivery, not protocols.
xDS adds a little overhead if anything — the win is live updates, not efficiency.

07-dynamic-config-xds.q: Match the API to what it discovers: LDS, CDS, EDS, RDS, SDS.
options: Listeners, Clusters, Endpoints, Routes, Secrets
Logs, Certificates, Endpoints, Rules, Sessions
Listeners, Certificates, Errors, Retries, Stats
Load, CPU, Events, Requests, Sockets
07-dynamic-config-xds.why: LDS=Listeners, RDS=Routes, CDS=Clusters, EDS=Endpoints, SDS=Secrets (TLS certs). ADS aggregates them all over one ordered stream.
whyWrong: Endpoints is right, but the other letters stand for Listeners, Clusters, Routes, and Secrets.
Errors, retries, and stats have no discovery services — xDS delivers config resources.
Those are machine metrics; xDS delivers Envoy config objects, not telemetry.

07-dynamic-config-xds.q: What is ADS and why would you prefer it?
options: Aggregated Discovery Service — all resources over one ordered stream, avoiding update races between separate streams
Automatic DNS Service — it resolves hostnames faster
Admin Debug Service — a richer version of the admin port
Asynchronous Data Store — a database for Envoy stats
07-dynamic-config-xds.why: Delivering LDS/RDS/CDS/EDS over separate streams can cause ordering races (e.g. a route referencing a cluster that hasn't arrived). ADS serializes them on one stream.
whyWrong: ADS has nothing to do with DNS — the A is 'Aggregated': one stream for all resource types.
The admin port is unrelated; ADS is part of the xDS config protocol.
Nothing is stored — ADS is a delivery channel, not a database.

07-dynamic-config-xds.q: Concretely, what is the data plane vs the control plane in an xDS setup?
options: Envoy subscribing to xDS is the data plane; the thing serving xDS (e.g. istiod) is the control plane
The data plane is the YAML file; the control plane is Docker
The data plane is the admin port; the control plane is the main listener
They are the same process
07-dynamic-config-xds.why: Envoy (data plane) subscribes and applies config. The control plane (e.g. istiod) watches the world and streams updates. This split is the whole mesh architecture.
whyWrong: The YAML file is static config, not a plane; Docker just runs the containers.
Both ports belong to the same Envoy — the planes are separate programs, not separate ports.
They're deliberately separate processes, usually on separate machines, talking over gRPC.

07-dynamic-config-xds.q: What happens when a control plane pushes an invalid configuration?
options: Envoy rejects the update and keeps serving the last good config
Envoy crashes and restarts
Envoy applies it anyway and drops all traffic
Envoy deletes its config and starts empty
07-dynamic-config-xds.why: Graceful rejection is a key safety property of xDS: a bad push doesn't take you down. If a change 'did nothing,' it was often rejected — check the update_rejected stats.
whyWrong: Envoy validates before applying; a bad push never brings the process down.
Invalid updates are never applied — that's precisely the failure xDS guards against.
The last good config stays active; Envoy never reverts to empty.

08-envoy-on-kubernetes.q: What are the three shapes Envoy takes on Kubernetes?
options: Edge gateway / ingress, service-mesh sidecar, and standalone Deployment
Pod, Service, and Namespace
Master, worker, and etcd
Frontend, backend, and database
08-envoy-on-kubernetes.why: Same binary, different topology: one pool at the edge (gateway), one next to every pod (mesh sidecar), or a hand-configured Deployment (rare, but shows the plumbing).
whyWrong: Those are Kubernetes primitives Envoy runs inside, not shapes Envoy takes.
That's the anatomy of a Kubernetes cluster's own components, not roles Envoy plays.
Those are application tiers; Envoy proxies between them rather than being one.

08-envoy-on-kubernetes.q: Why did the Gateway API replace the older Kubernetes Ingress resource?
options: Typed resources plus a clean split between infra-owned Gateways and app-owned Routes — no annotation soup
It is faster at forwarding packets
Ingress only worked with nginx
Gateway API removed the need for any controller
08-envoy-on-kubernetes.why: Ingress leaned on vendor-specific annotations and had no good multi-team story. Gateway API splits responsibilities: platform teams own GatewayClass/Gateway, app teams own HTTPRoute.
whyWrong: Forwarding speed depends on the proxy underneath, which is the same either way.
Ingress had many implementations — that was the problem: each needed its own annotations.
A controller is still required; the API defines intent, and something must implement it.

08-envoy-on-kubernetes.q: Which Gateway API resource do application teams typically write?
options: HTTPRoute — the routing rules that attach to a Gateway
GatewayClass — which controller implements gateways
Node — a cluster machine
PersistentVolume — storage
08-envoy-on-kubernetes.why: App teams own HTTPRoute (match paths/headers → their Service). The platform team owns the Gateway (entry point, ports, TLS) and the GatewayClass (which controller).
whyWrong: GatewayClass is cluster-level plumbing owned by the platform team.
Nodes are machines managed by cluster operators, not routing config.
Storage has nothing to do with HTTP routing.

08-envoy-on-kubernetes.q: What does Envoy Gateway actually do with your Gateway and HTTPRoute YAML?
options: Translates it into Envoy xDS config and programs the data-plane Envoys
Compiles it into a container image
Stores it in a database and does nothing else
Runs it directly as a shell script
08-envoy-on-kubernetes.why: Envoy Gateway is a control plane: it watches your Gateway API objects and generates the corresponding Envoy xDS (listeners, routes, clusters) for the proxies it manages.
whyWrong: No images are built — the same Envoy image runs; only its config changes.
It stores nothing passively; watching and translating into xDS is its entire job.
The YAML is declarative data describing intent, not an executable script.

08-envoy-on-kubernetes.q: When you scale a Deployment from 2 to 4 replicas, how does Envoy learn about the new pods?
options: The control plane pushes updated endpoints via EDS — no config edit needed
You must manually restart Envoy
You edit the envoy.yaml file and redeploy
Envoy never learns; you must recreate the Gateway
08-envoy-on-kubernetes.why: This is Module 07 made real: you change a Kubernetes object, the control plane notices, and streams new endpoints to the data-plane Envoy over EDS. No file editing.
whyWrong: No restart needed — endpoint updates stream in live over EDS.
There's no file to edit; the control plane generates config from cluster state.
The Gateway object is untouched; only the endpoint set behind the Service changed.

09-service-mesh-sidecars.q: What makes something a service mesh rather than just an edge gateway?
options: An Envoy on every workload handling all service-to-service traffic, not just traffic at the edge
It runs on more powerful servers
It only handles HTTPS
It replaces Kubernetes entirely
09-service-mesh-sidecars.why: A mesh applies Envoy's routing, resilience, security, and observability to EVERY internal call by giving each workload its own proxy — not just the front door.
whyWrong: Hardware isn't the distinction — topology is: a proxy at every workload vs one at the door.
A mesh handles whatever its proxies understand, including plain HTTP and raw TCP.
A mesh runs ON Kubernetes (or VMs); it complements the orchestrator, never replaces it.

09-service-mesh-sidecars.q: Which of these does a mesh give you with no application code changes?
options: mTLS everywhere, traffic policy/retries/canaries, and uniform observability
Automatic database sharding
Free compute capacity
A new programming language for your services
09-service-mesh-sidecars.why: Because both ends of every call are Envoys, the mesh uniformly provides encryption+identity, traffic management, telemetry, and authorization — all by config, not app code.
whyWrong: Sharding is a data-layer design problem; the mesh only touches traffic between services.
A mesh consumes extra compute for its proxies — it gives features, not capacity.
Services keep their languages; the mesh's whole pitch is being language-agnostic.

09-service-mesh-sidecars.q: What is the key difference between sidecar mode and ambient mode?
options: Sidecar = a full Envoy in every pod; ambient = a per-node Rust L4 proxy (ztunnel) plus per-namespace Envoy waypoints for L7
Sidecar uses TCP; ambient uses UDP
Ambient removes Envoy entirely
They are two names for the same architecture
09-service-mesh-sidecars.why: Ambient mode moves the proxy out of every pod: ztunnel (Rust) handles cheap per-node mTLS/L4, and Envoy waypoints add L7 only where needed. Envoy is still the L7 engine.
whyWrong: Both modes carry ordinary TCP traffic; the difference is where the proxies live.
Envoy remains as the L7 waypoint; only the per-pod copies go away.
They're distinct architectures — per-pod proxies vs a shared per-node layer plus waypoints.

09-service-mesh-sidecars.q: How does a sidecar transparently intercept its app's traffic?
options: iptables rules redirect the pod's inbound/outbound traffic to the local Envoy's ports; the app is unaware
The app must be recompiled to call Envoy directly
Envoy edits the app's source code at runtime
The app sends traffic to a central Envoy over the internet
09-service-mesh-sidecars.why: An init container programs iptables so every packet detours through the local Envoy (commonly :15001 outbound, :15006 inbound). The app thinks it's talking straight to the peer.
whyWrong: No rebuild needed — transparency is the point; the redirect happens at the network layer.
Envoy never touches app code; iptables reroutes the packets underneath it.
The sidecar is local to the pod; traffic detours within the pod, not across the internet.

09-service-mesh-sidecars.q: What programs all those sidecar Envoys?
options: The control plane — e.g. istiod — via xDS
Each app configures its own sidecar
A human edits every sidecar's YAML by hand
They are not configured at all
09-service-mesh-sidecars.why: istiod watches the Kubernetes API and streams LDS/RDS/CDS/EDS/SDS to every sidecar, keyed by the pod's identity. Same xDS mechanism from Module 07, at fleet scale.
whyWrong: Apps are unaware of their sidecar; configuration comes from outside, not from the workload.
Hand-editing thousands of sidecars is exactly what xDS automation exists to avoid.
Sidecars are richly configured — routes, certs, and endpoints all streamed via xDS.

10-debugging-gotchas-next-steps.q: What is the first place to look when debugging a bad response?
options: The access-log line and its %RESPONSE_FLAGS% code
The source code of the backend service
The Docker image build logs
The operating system kernel logs
10-debugging-gotchas-next-steps.why: The access log has the response code and a short flag explaining WHY the request ended that way — usually the answer before you look anywhere else.
whyWrong: Reading backend code is a last resort — the proxy's log usually names the failure directly.
Build logs tell you about image creation, nothing about a live request.
Kernel logs sit far below the layer where routing and upstream errors live.

10-debugging-gotchas-next-steps.q: You get an 'NR' response flag. What are two likely causes?
options: No route matched — a bad or wrongly-ordered match, or the Host isn't in the virtual_host domains
The backend is out of memory, or the disk is full
TLS certificate expired, or the port is wrong
Too many retries, or a circuit breaker tripped
10-debugging-gotchas-next-steps.why: NR = no route configured. Either your match is wrong / sits below a catch-all, or the request's Host header isn't covered by any virtual_host's domains.
whyWrong: Backend resource problems would still route — you'd see UT or a 5xx, not NR.
TLS or port problems fail after routing succeeds; NR means no route ever matched.
Retry exhaustion and circuit breaking have their own flags; NR is purely a routing miss.

10-debugging-gotchas-next-steps.q: You get a 'UH' response flag. What should you check?
options: /clusters — endpoint health, ejection state, the cluster address, and health checks
The client's browser version
The route ordering only
The admin port number
10-debugging-gotchas-next-steps.why: UH = no healthy upstream. All endpoints are unhealthy/ejected, or the cluster address is wrong. /clusters shows each endpoint's health and ejection state.
whyWrong: UH is server-side: the request routed fine but found no healthy endpoint to use.
Routing already succeeded — UH means the chosen cluster has nothing healthy in it.
The admin port is where you'd look (/clusters), not the thing that's broken.

10-debugging-gotchas-next-steps.q: Your xDS change 'did nothing.' What most likely happened?
options: Envoy rejected an invalid update and kept the last good config — check the update_rejected stats/logs
Envoy silently deleted the change
Kubernetes blocked the request
The change applied but curl cached the old response forever
10-debugging-gotchas-next-steps.why: A bad push is rejected so it can't take you down. 'My change did nothing' usually means 'my change was invalid' — look for *.update_rejected in the stats.
whyWrong: Envoy doesn't delete pushed config; it refuses invalid updates and counts the rejection.
Kubernetes isn't in the xDS path between the control plane and Envoy.
curl doesn't cache; the stale behavior is Envoy still serving its last good config.

10-debugging-gotchas-next-steps.q: Recite the noun chain from port to backend.
options: listener → filter chain → HCM/HTTP filters → router → route → cluster → endpoint
cluster → route → listener → endpoint → filter chain
endpoint → router → listener → cluster → route
route → cluster → listener → filter chain → endpoint
10-debugging-gotchas-next-steps.why: That chain IS Envoy. A listener binds a port, the filter chain's HCM runs HTTP filters ending in the router, which uses the route table to pick a cluster, which balances to an endpoint.
whyWrong: Clusters come after routing — nothing starts at the cluster.
The endpoint is the destination, the last link in the chain, never the first.
Routes are consulted inside the listener's HTTP processing, not before the listener.

11-rate-limiting-ext-authz.q: Ten Envoy sidecars each run a local rate limit of 100 rps. What is the actual cap on total traffic to the backend?
options: 100 rps
1,000 rps — local limits are per proxy instance; a global promise needs a shared rate limit service with one counter
10 rps
Unlimited
11-rate-limiting-ext-authz.why: 'Local' means each Envoy owns its own token bucket. Ten buckets of 100 = 1,000. Customer-facing quotas ('1,000/hour per API key') require the global filter and a central counting service.
whyWrong: That would require the proxies to share a bucket — exactly what local limiting doesn't do.
Limits don't divide across instances; they multiply.
Each instance does enforce its own 100 — traffic isn't unlimited, just 10× the naïve reading.

11-rate-limiting-ext-authz.q: Why is enforcing authentication in an ext_authz filter better than middleware in every service?
options: It's faster than any library
The filter runs before routing for every request, so no endpoint can forget the check — enforcement is structural, not a per-team convention
It eliminates the need for tokens
It encrypts the requests
11-rate-limiting-ext-authz.why: The proxy enforces, the authz service decides. Every service that 'didn't add the middleware' is a breach waiting to happen; a filter in the chain removes that failure mode by construction.
whyWrong: Speed is comparable; the win is coverage, not latency.
Tokens are still validated — by the check service; ext_authz is how the answer is enforced.
TLS handles encryption; ext_authz handles decisions.

11-rate-limiting-ext-authz.q: Why does the conventional filter order put authentication BEFORE rate limiting?
options: Alphabetical convention
So limits can count identities (API keys, users) instead of IPs — an attacker has many IPs, but a free-tier key is one key no matter the botnet
Rate limiting doesn't work first
To make 401s faster than 429s
11-rate-limiting-ext-authz.why: Order is policy: authenticate first and the limiter's descriptors can be who is calling rather than where from — which is the difference between a quota and a speed bump.
whyWrong: Filter order is explicit configuration with semantic meaning.
Either order runs; one of them just counts the wrong thing.
Status-code latency is not the design driver.
